- When sentiment shows strong negative signals (e.g., -1.00) in recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >70% from prior 30d mean), model often overshoots and fails to correct — apply downward bias or introduce mean-reversion decay factor.
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (0.00–0.50) and price is trending upward, model often overestimates — cap forecast growth rate at 1–2% per day.
- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., 1.00) and price is near support, model tends to ignore support — add a floor constraint or reduce upward drift.
- Model consistently overestimates in early 30d forecasts when sentiment is mixed or volatile — apply smoothing filter or use 3-day moving average for initial 5–7 days.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 70) after a spike, model often fails to recognize — reduce forecast slope by 20–30% for 3–5 days post-spike.
- Sentiment history with alternating +/– signals (e.g., 0.50, -1.00, 1.00) suggests model is overfitting to recent noise — apply sentiment-weighted smoothing (e.g., 50% recent, 50% 30d average).
